title: Seven Days Without Public Praise
script: Narrator: [warmly] For one week, our volunteer team tried an unusual experiment: nobody would post photographs of their own contribution. We could report what the project needed, but we would not turn every donated meal or packed box into personal publicity.

Narrator: I expected the rule to feel simple. By the second day, I understood how much I had depended on visible appreciation. When friends asked what I was doing after work, I wanted to show them proof that my time mattered.

Narrator: [reflective] The absence of praise also exposed a second problem. We had been choosing tasks that looked impressive on camera while avoiding quiet jobs such as checking expiry dates, cleaning containers, and updating the delivery list.

Narrator: On Wednesday, I spent two hours correcting addresses. Nobody applauded, but three drivers later said the revised list prevented wasted journeys. The usefulness of the task had not changed; only its visibility had.

Narrator: [carefully] Our coordinator reminded us that hidden service is not automatically sincere, and visible service is not automatically wrong. Intentions belong to the person and are known fully only to Allah. The exercise was simply a way to examine our habits without judging one another.
Narrator: By Friday, we had begun thanking people for specific contributions in private. The messages felt more meaningful than a general post because they named the care behind the work.
Narrator: [thoughtful] When the week ended, we did publish one update—with consent, no identifying details about recipients, and a focus on the remaining need rather than on our faces.
Narrator: I learned that good character grows through repeated choices: doing necessary work, protecting people's dignity, and accepting that not every valuable action needs an audience.

quiz.question: What rule did volunteers follow for one week?
options: They avoided posting photographs of their own service
quiz.explanation: The experiment removed personal publicity, not useful reporting.

quiz.question: What did the narrator discover by day two?
options: The project had no remaining needs
Visible appreciation had become personally important
quiz.explanation: The urge to show proof revealed dependence on praise.

quiz.question: Which work had volunteers been avoiding?
options: Quiet tasks such as checking dates and addresses
quiz.explanation: Less visible maintenance had received less attention.

quiz.question: How did corrected addresses help?
quiz.explanation: The unseen task improved delivery efficiency.

quiz.question: Why did the coordinator reject judging intentions?
options: Only Allah fully knows what is in a person's heart
quiz.explanation: The exercise examined habits without claiming inner knowledge.

quiz.question: What kind of thanks replaced general public praise?
quiz.explanation: Private thanks named particular care without performance.

quiz.question: How did the final public update protect recipients?
options: It used consent and omitted identifying details
quiz.explanation: The update focused on need rather than exposure.

quiz.question: What balance does the narrator recognise?
options: Visible service is not automatically wrong
quiz.explanation: Visibility alone cannot establish a person's intention.

quiz.question: Which action best fits the experiment's lesson?
options: Complete necessary work even when nobody sees it
Choose tasks with the best photographs
Assume quiet volunteers are more sincere
quiz.explanation: Value should not depend on an audience.

quiz.question: What broader quality does the week cultivate?
quiz.explanation: The narrator links good character to service, privacy, and consistency.
